newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Deutsche Telekom up on 1996 report.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Deutsche Telekom up on 1996 report.

text.p: German telecommunications group Deutsche Telekom AG, hoping to give a boost to its beleaguered shares, caught the market by surprise on Monday with a statement that business in 1996 was better than expected.

Although unusual for a German company to report on its business so soon after the turn of the year, as Telekom's shares touched new lows last week investors urged the company to give the market more information about its performance.

Two months after its landmark $13 billion listing, German media commentators were saying the hopes of nearly two million ordinary Germans who had bought Telekom shares were in danger of fading as the share price continued falling.

But with the market not expecting any new information until March, Telekom issued a statement which said group sales rose nearly six percent to 63 billion marks ($38.7 billion) on an adjusted basis and profit had beaten the company's forecasts.
"Deutsche Telekom will exceed previous estimates for the full year," chairman Ron Sommer said in the statement. "All in all the board's expectations have been more than fulfilled."
Sales were slighlty higher than analysts forecasts and the well-timed statement packed the intended punch.

Telekom shares rose as high as 31.69 marks in Frankfurt and closed bourse trade at 31.56 marks, up 1.41 percent and outperforming the DAX list of 30 blue-chips which was up 0.98 percent to 3030.68 points.
One analyst at a London-based investment bank, who asked not to be identified, said he had forecast turnover of 62.5 billion marks and pre-tax profit of 4.2 billion marks in 1996.
"The figures are higher than what I or other analysts have been expecting and could mean that revenue in the second half of the year recovered more strongly than anticipated," he said.
Deutsche Telekom sales in the first half of 1996 were hit by two factors.

On the one hand the company became liable for value added tax (VAT) for the first time but decided not to pass on the charge to customers. This meant the company had to digest an effective fall in revenue of around 6.5 billion marks.
The six percent rise in 1996 revenue comes about by adjusting 1995 sales as if Deutsche Telekom had paid VAT that year, giving a total of 59.5 billion marks, the company said.

The company previously reported group sales of 66.1 billion marks and operating profit of 10.3 billion marks. Ahead of the November listing Telekom management indicated operating profit could fall this year to around six billion marks.

A second factor that put pressure on revenues was a new set of tariffs that lowered long-distance calls but raised local calls that came into effect in January last year. The highly-publicised rate hikes led to a drop in call volumes.
"These things had a negative effect on revenue in the first half of the year and it now seems that usage had already normalised by July or August," one analyst said.
While the company's statement was short on detail, it seemed to press all the right buttons for investors.

It said the high level of cash flow allowed it to finance investment and still cut debt to 82 billion marks at the end of 1996, a decline of 10 billion marks from 1995. The workforce fell to 201,000 employees at the end of 1996, half-way to its target of 170,000 by the year 2000.

"It is positive that Telekom issued this statement so soon. That will help the share price," said Commerzbank analyst Sabine Schauer. She raised her profit forecast to 2.10 marks for 1997 from 1.90 and to 2.50 marks for 1998 from 2.40.
Klaus Repges of Trinkaus Capital Management said it was difficult to assess the statement because Telekom management in the past has been so vague about its own expectations.
"The numbers are not very meaningful because there have been no concrete statements about profit ahead of time," he said, adding that he would continue to recommend "underweight".
